Plant Vogtle Units 3 & 4Semi-Annual Construction Monitoring ReportAugust 2009Docket No. 29849-U EXECUTIVE SUMMARY  Pursuant to the stipulation (the  Stipulation ) adopted in the Georgia Public Service Commission s (the  Commission ) Order in Docket Number 27800-U ( Certification Order ), Georgia Power Company ( Georgia Power  or the  Company ) submits this Semi-Annual Construction Monitoring Report (the  Report ) to the Commission.
Section 2(c) of the Stipulation requires the Report to be filed semi-annually, with the first Report due on August 31, 2009.  This is the first of those reports.This executive summary provides an overview of the information contained in the Report, and supports the Company s assertion that construction of new units 3 and 4 at Plant Vogtle (the  Units ) (sometimes referred to as the  Project ) is on schedule and on budget, and demonstrates that cost pressures are being actively and prudently managed.   The body of this Report responds to the 15 items the Stipulation specified would be addressed in each report.  However, several key developments and issues should be highlighted to put the Project s progress in context. The Project is on schedule.  A Level 1 Schedule showing progress to date against the milestones is Exhibit 1 to this Report.  To provide more than just a snapshot view of the Project, the Company has also incorporated into this Report the information from the Monthly Reports submitted to the Commission by Georgia Power and the Engineering Procurement and Construction ( EPC ) Status Reports submitted to Georgia Power, Oglethorpe Power Corporation, Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia and the City of Dalton (the  Co-Owners ) by Westinghouse Electric Company LLC ( Westinghouse ) and Stone & Webster, Inc. (together with Westinghouse, the  Consortium ) during the same period.  The June 2009 Monthly Report is Exhibit 2  and the June 2009 EPC Status Report is Exhibit 3.  The Company points out however, that the EPC Status Reports are prepared by the Consortium and the Company does not necessarily endorse every position taken in those reports.  The Company continues to exercise prudent control over the Project.  The Company and its Co-Owners retained PricewaterhouseCoopers ( PWC ) to conduct a  readiness review  which was a thorough, risk-based assessment of project management, financial reporting and oversight. This review began in 2008 and continued into the first quarter of 2009.  It resulted in several key observations and recommendations that have been incorporated into the project management structure and adopted into the Company s financial reporting procedures.   PWC has also been retained to serve as an Independent Project Advisor.  PWC will provide an independent evaluation of Project governance and control structure, and provide senior management with assessments against best industry practices.  PWC will also provide contract administration support by reviewing data supplied by vendors for compliance with contract terms and conditions.The Company has adopted a streamlined and effective project management structure that includes the creation of an Executive Vice President of Nuclear Development position that reports directly to the CEOs of Georgia Power and Southern Nuclear.  The Vogtle Project Management Board, which includes senior executive representatives from the Company and the Co-Owners, was established to act as the highly integrated senior management oversight board. In addition, a Vogtle Expansion Oversight Committee ( VEOC ) was created that draws together senior Southern Company executives.  The VEOC is chaired by the CEO of Georgia Power, co-Chaired by the CEO of Southern Nuclear, and includes the CEO of Southern Company, the CFO of Southern Company, and the COO of Southern Company.  The Executive Vice President of Nuclear Development and the General Counsel of Southern Company also participate in the VEOC.
 One primary consideration for the Project is the safety of the work force.  The Project has had one recordable safety event in 2009.  It had none in 2008.  The most significant licensing development was the issuance of the Early Site Permit ( ESP ) and the Limited Work Authorization on August 26, 2009.  While the Company recognizes that this is beyond the scope of this Report (this Report covers activities through June 30, 2009) it is such a significant event that it would render a discussion of the ESP progress as it existed on June 30th irrelevant.  The Company and the Consortium continue to finalize the Design Control Documents ( DCD ) at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission ( NRC ) and the Combined Operating License Application ( COLA ) review remains on schedule.  The Company has responded to over 1,600 requests for additional information from the NRC.  The Company is watching and managing several areas of exposure to the schedule and cost, but as of now it believes the Project will stay on budget and on schedule from a licensing perspective.Overall, engineering continues to be on schedule and on budget.  While some engineering items are behind schedule, none affect the critical path, and recovery plans are in place for those items.  The turbine building is being extended as compared to the original design to allow for increased space for turbine operating and maintenance activities.  Design finalization is expected to be essentially complete in April 2011.Construction activities continue to be on schedule and on budget. Top soil removal began June 22, 2009.  Heave and settlement monitoring equipment was being installed for Unit 3 as of June 30th, with installation of Unit 4 equipment commencing in July. Major excavation begins after heave and settlement monitoring equipment is installed. The Consortium continues the procurement of major components and contractors.  So far it has awarded REDACTED contracts, REDACTED of which are within the Southern Company territory, and REDACTED of those REDACTED are within 100 miles of the Project site.Table 1.1 reflects the status of the Project s budget as of June 30th. During the certification proceeding, the Company promised to lower the in-service cost of the Project from $6.4 billion to $4.529 billion if the Company s request to include Construction Work In Progress ( CWIP ) in rate base was granted.  The Company has kept that commitment in this filing.  However, because SB 31 will collect the 2009 and 2010 financing costs slightly differently than proposed by the Company in its certification request, there is an additional $REDACTED which is now set aside for contingency.  If it is not used, of course, the in-service cost will be even lower than $4.529 billion.While no EPC change orders have been approved to date, and while the Project continues to be on schedule and on budget, that is not to suggest that this is not a complex and large project with daily management challenges.
Many issues are being managed and watched, some of which could put pressure on the schedule and budget.  Among those items is finalization of the DCD, which could impact the progress of the COLA. The change is a result of the impact of placing CWIP into rate base as authorized by the Commission s Certification Order for construction of the new Units, and as supported by SB 31.  Initially, the Company requested that the Commission allow it to place CWIP in rate base beginning on January 1, 2011 and otherwise accrue Allowance for Funds Used During Construction ( AFUDC ) from the time of certification through December 31, 2010.  The accrued AFUDC amount would have been recovered in rates after the Units were in commercial operation.  However, the provisions of SB 31 require the Company to recover the AFUDC accrued through December 31, 2010 in rates over the five (5) year period from 2011 through 2015.  The accrued AFUDC at December 31, 2010 is projected to total $REDACTED.
This $REDACTED will be held in contingency should such funds be needed, as shown in Table 1.1 below.

These groups provide forums for builders of a given technology type to consider issues common to the participants, including possible labor issues.  Currently, labor issues are addressed via joint training standards and programs that are being developed between the members of the groups. The groups operate under strict anti-trust rules and do not collaborate in any way to influence the labor markets. An explanation of how the indices used in the EPC contract are tracking.The REDACTED and REDACTED are currently tracking REDACTED estimates, as shown in Tables 3.1 and 3.2. There is no change at this time to the estimate provided in October 2008.  In November 2008, Southern Nuclear executed a contract with the Department of Energy  ( DOE ) that requires the DOE to complete removal of spent fuel from Vogtle Units 3 and 4 within ten (10) years from the date of the shutdown of Unit 4. The status of the Company s loan guarantee application at the Department of Energy and to the extent that application is granted, then the Company shall also report on the impact it has or would have on the final expected in-service cost of the units. The Company filed part one of its application to the DOE for loan guarantees on September 29, 2008 and filed part two on December 19, 2008.  The Company submitted the 90 day updates required by the DOE on March 19, 2009 and on June 17, 2009.The DOE is authorized to provide loan guarantees of up to $18.5 billion.  The Company is requesting up to $REDACTED.The DOE Credit Review Board has approved the Project as one of the approved projects that will proceed to advanced due diligence.  Advanced due diligence will begin in the fall of 2009.  As discussed in item 1, since all financing costs will be recovered through rates during the construction period, the ultimate in-service cost of the Units will not be impacted by the availability of the loan guarantees.No projects have been approved by DOE for loan guarantees at this time.  Whether the Company is using trust preferred financing and the impact it has or would have on the expected in-service cost of the units.The Company has not issued trust preferred financing since 2004 and currently has no plans to do so.  The Company does not currently view trust preferred financing to be an economic financing choice.  This view is based on the high cost of trust preferred financing compared to senior note financing and the low level of equity treatment awarded it by the major credit rating agencies.  The Company continues to monitor the security markets and update its financial policies as needed in an effort to minimize overall financing costs for customers.The extent to which the Company is using short term debt and the impact it has or would have on the expected in-service cost of the units.Under a prior stipulation with the Commission, the Company has been directed to first apply its short term debt balances towards financing of under-recovered fuel balances before directing the remaining balances to finance CWIP.  Through June 2009, substantially all short term debt has been applied to the under-recovered fuel balances.  However, as discussed in item 1, since all financing costs will be recovered through rates during the construction period, the ultimate in-service cost of the Units will not reflect the impact of either short term or long term debt financing. An update of the estimated in-service cost and projected date of commercial operation of both units. An update of the estimated in-service cost of both Units is shown in Table 8.1 below. The scheduled approved in the certification of the Units provides for a commercial operation date ("COD") for Unit 3 in April, 2016 and a COD for Unit 4 in April, 2017. The status of procurement, engineering, fabrication, transportation and erection of major equipment. Consortium Responsibilities.  Under the EPC Agreement for the construction of the new Units 3 and 4, the Consortium has the responsibility for all activities involving the procurement, engineering, fabrication, transportation and erection of major equipment.  Georgia Power, through its agent Southern Nuclear, is overseeing those activities to confirm that the Consortium is abiding by the terms of the EPC Agreement and that the Project meets the standards of quality demanded by Georgia Power.  As part of the Owner s oversight function, Georgia Power, through its agent Southern Nuclear has developed a Procurement Project Manager position. The responsibilities of this position include developing and implementing a strategy for the Vendor Technical Surveillance Program as well as managing Supply Chain activities.  The position will also ensure that the equipment needed for the Units fully meets the technical and schedule requirements including transportation that are necessary to support schedule commitments and provide for long-term reliability of the new Units.Status of Procurement.
The Consortium s current procurement activities are proceeding in a manner that is consistent with meeting the Project schedule. The June 2009 EPC Status Report provides detailed information regarding the status of procurement. Engineering.  Engineering activities supporting the completion of the Westinghouse AP1000 standard design continue on schedule. The June 2009 EPC Status Report provides detailed information regarding the status of engineering. The economic analysis performed for this Report has relied on the methodologies and assumptions used in the economic evaluations conducted in Docket 27800-U.  Based on the evidence presented in that docket, the Commission approved Georgia Power s application for the certification of the Units as modified by the Stipulation between the Commission Staff and the Company.  Given that the Commission certified the Units less than six months ago, many of the key inputs are the same, or, are currently in the process of being updated. Two key factors have been updated for the economic evaluation included in this Report.  These are the projected costs to complete the Units and the Company s cost of debt.  The projected costs in this economic evaluation include the additional costs for spent fuel storage as described in item 4 above.  The Company s cost of debt is projected to be lower than was assumed in the evaluations conducted in Docket No. 27800-U.  The other factors that are inputs to the economic analysis are currently being reviewed or updated as a part of the Company s research and analysis for the 2010 Integrated Resource Plan that will be filed in January 2010.  The February 2010 Semi-Annual Construction Monitoring Report will include the results of the economic evaluation using these updated factors. The economic evaluation for the period ending August 2009 compares the costs to complete, operate, and maintain the Units versus the costs to build, operate, and maintain the alternative gas-fired CC unit or units over the same useful life.
Sunk costs  (non-refundable costs already incurred or projected to have been incurred as of August 31, 2009) are excluded from this forward-looking analysis. The relative economics for the Units, when compared to the gas-fired alternative, vary depending on the assumptions for future fuel prices and cost associated with potential future carbon legislation.  In the cases involving some form of future carbon legislation and mid-fuel forecasts or higher, the Project saves customers from $REDACTED to $REDACTED (see Table 14.1 below).  In the less likely case of no future carbon legislation and low fuel prices throughout the expected 60 year life of the Units, natural gas CC generation would save customers about $REDACTED.  At the same time, construction of a gas-fired power plant to meet the specific capacity needs in 2016 and 2017 has significant risks, as the continued reliance on natural gas-fired generation increases customers  exposure to volatile natural gas prices.  The fuel price cases represent a wide range of possible future fuel prices.  The potential costs for future carbon legislation were developed by the Company.  The  $REDACTED CO2  case and the  $REDACTED CO2  case assumed the costs to comply with potential carbon legislation will equal $REDACTED and $REDACTED above inflation until REDACTED when carbon costs escalate with general inflation rates.  Table 14.1 below shows the difference in lifetime costs of building, operating, and maintaining the gas-fired alternative less the lifetime costs of completing, operating, and maintaining Units 3 and 4, with positive savings figures meaning Units 3 and 4 are cheaper than the gas alternative, and similarly, negative savings figures in Table 14.1 meaning the gas alternative is cheaper than Units 3 and 4. Table 14.1
 Relative Savings of Units 3 and 4 versus CC as of August 31, 2009 Incremental Cost to Complete (Net present value of lifetime costs of CC minus Units 3 and 4)Fuel \ CO2 $0 CO2 $REDACTED CO2 $REDACTED CO2  High Fuel REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED  SCS 2009 Fcst REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED  Mid Fuel REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED  Low Fuel REDACTED N/A N/A  This analysis shown in Table 14.1 is an economic assessment from an  incremental cost to complete  perspective, which ignores any potential cancellation fees or other costs that would be incurred if the project were stopped as well as any fully-committed construction costs that would not be avoidable in the event the project is cancelled.  If the results from the incremental cost to complete evaluation showed it was no longer cost-effective to pursue completing the Units, a second  cancellation  assessment would have been performed to determine the economic value of canceling the Units.  The  cancellation  assessment would provide the most appropriate perspective for deciding whether to cancel the Units as it would include the incremental costs to complete the Units along with the impacts of any cancellation fees or other costs associated with canceling the project.  Table 14.1 shows significant savings and benefits to customers from the incremental cost to complete perspective across a wide range of possible future fuel prices and carbon costs.  Therefore, a cancellation assessment is not required at this time.  The Company will be under a continuing obligation to supplement its response to PIA Staff DR STF-TN-1-2 by ensuring that the financing data reflected in the schedules attached to that DR response reflect the most current and updated information at the time of each semi-annual monitoring report.  In addition, the Company will provide the most current information shared with each of the Rating Agencies. To comply with this requirement, the Company is including Trade Secret Exhibits 4 through 6, which provide the following information in vintage order:Presentations provided to the major Rating Agencies at the Company s annual rating agency meeting held on May 19, 2009 in Atlanta, Georgia.  Attached as Exhibit 4a is the printed booklet provided to participants and Exhibit 4b is the visual aid presentation.An update of Georgia Power s financial projections for the period 2009 through 2013 including the projected annual income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, attached as Exhibit 5.An update to the schedule of Financing Issuances and Balances for the Project through 2020 under CWIP in rate base methodology, attached as Exhibit 6. EXHIBIT 1Level 1 Schedule REDACTED IN ITS ENTIRETY EXHIBIT 2June Monthly ReportSee Attached Exhibit EXHIBIT 3EPC Status ReportREDACTED IN ITS ENTIRETY EXHIBIT 4Presentation to major rating agencies at the Company s annual rating agency meeting held on May 19, 2009 in Atlanta, GeorgiaREDACTED IN ITS ENTIRETY EXHIBIT 5Update of Georgia Power financial projections for the period 2009 through 2013 including projected annual income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement.REDACTED IN ITS ENTIRETY EXHIBIT 6An update to the schedule of Financing Issuances and Balances for the Project through 2020 under CWIP in Rate base methodology.REDACTED IN ITS ENTIRETY  The June 2009 Monthly Report attached as Exhibit 2 to this Report includes the corrected data to the Level 1 Critical Path schedule.
